slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Choice, Self-Direction, and a Life Beyond Services
Explore meaningful choice, chosen support, and the difference between a service delivered and the life a person wants.
Foundation self-directed learning
slides.narration: Services can support a life without becoming its whole description. A person may value relationships, creative work, a chosen home, or the opportunity to direct everyday decisions. This course examines how self-direction and meaningful choice keep those purposes visible. service, workplace, and community situations help you compare options and notice when familiar arrangements close inquiry too soon. Actual program responsibilities and constraints remain. The learning does not authorize a service or settle a person’s decision; it helps you ask more useful questions.

slides.text:
A schedule is not the whole life
A familiar activity fills the calendar. The person wants a different experience connected to their interests.

A full schedule may still miss relationships, choice, or a sense of purpose.

What would you need to understand before calling the schedule a good result?
slides.narration: A delivered activity is something the service can record. Whether that activity fits the person’s desired life is another question. Imagine wanting to make music with friends while the schedule offers a demonstration to watch alone. Both involve music, but they are not the same experience. Repeating that broad substitution can make attendance the measure while the person’s purpose disappears. Ask what matters within the activity and which details an appropriate comparison needs, without presuming the unfamiliar option is available.

slides.text:
Self-direction concerns meaningful influence
Self-direction means a person has a meaningful role in choosing and directing support within the applicable arrangement.

Support can help a decision without taking it over.

A general principle does not settle eligibility, funding, legal authority, or program-specific responsibilities.
slides.narration: The central question is who influences the support and how. A person may want more control over timing, relationships, or how an activity is arranged. They may also want help understanding options and managing the practical work involved. Self-direction should not be reduced to doing everything alone or to unlimited choice. Actual program arrangements have responsibilities and constraints. This introductory learning keeps influence visible while leaving formal requirements and decisions with the appropriate process and responsible people.

slides.text:
The familiar menu can close inquiry early
A person wants to participate in a community music group. Staff offer only the activity already on the service schedule.

The shortcut may replace the desired relationship and contribution. Repetition can make unfamiliar goals hard to pursue.

Clarify the purpose, compare real options, and name what needs further inquiry.
slides.narration: The existing activity may have value, but that does not establish that it serves this person’s purpose. A community music group could involve participation, relationships, or a role that the scheduled activity does not offer. Staff should understand those differences before treating the options as interchangeable. The next choice asks how to compare them within actual responsibilities. No funding, transport, or participation arrangement is established in the fiction. Taking the goal seriously means asking accurately, not promising the outcome in advance.

slides.text:
A goal beyond the existing activity
A person wants to play music with a community group. Staff offer only the familiar listening activity on the service schedule. What would best support a meaningful comparison?
A. Clarify what matters, describe the real options, and identify support and unanswered availability questions.
B. Treat both activities as identical because they involve music.
C. Promise the community option before checking support, availability, or actual responsibilities.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The person’s request identifies a possibility beyond the familiar schedule, but the case does not establish exactly why it matters. Playing might involve contribution, relationships, or creative choice. Listening may offer something useful while missing those features. Consider how to compare without reducing the goal to a label or promising an arrangement before the necessary inquiry. Actual responsibilities and limits remain. A meaningful question can make the person’s purpose visible, with support needs, availability, and the eventual decision still open rather than assumed from the request.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Clarify what matters, describe the real options, and identify support and unanswered availability questions.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Treat both activities as identical because they involve music.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Promise the community option before checking support, availability, or actual responsibilities.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This preserves the purpose while keeping options and limits honest. It may interrupt a menu-first routine that narrows choice. Use appropriate inquiry; the arrangement and preferred option remain unsettled.

Which difference between playing and listening matters to the person?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Clarifying purpose helps compare the actual experiences rather than only the category. The person can explain what matters while appropriate roles examine support and availability. If repeated, this approach may reduce a default that treats the current menu as the whole life goal. The response does not authorize a service, guarantee the community activity, or establish which option the person will choose after receiving useful information.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The label hides participation and relationship differences. Repetition may count attendance while missing the desired life. Ask about the meaning and compare relevant features; the person’s priorities are not established by the label.

Which difference between playing and listening matters to the person?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Both options concern music, but that does not make them interchangeable. The person may want to contribute or be part of a relationship that the listening activity does not offer. Repeating the broad substitution can make attendance the success measure while the desired experience disappears. Ask about relevant features and real options. Neither the complete purpose nor the value of each option is settled by the label.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
An unchecked promise may create expectations staff cannot meet. Repetition can weaken trust in choice conversations. Take the goal seriously through appropriate inquiry; approval, support, and availability remain unknown.

Which difference between playing and listening matters to the person?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A promise can sound supportive yet mislead when availability and responsibilities have not been examined. If repeated, such promises may make choice conversations less trustworthy. The goal deserves serious inquiry through the appropriate process, with clear information about what is known and unresolved. This case does not establish support, funding, approval, or the eventual experience, so those cannot be described as guaranteed.

slides.text:
Independent living is about control, not isolation
The independent living movement emphasizes disabled people’s influence over their lives and participation in community.

Using assistance can be consistent with directing a decision.

Do not equate independence with the absence of relationships or support.
slides.narration: People commonly rely on others while retaining control over their own priorities. The independent living perspective challenges the assumption that professionals should make every important choice because someone needs support. It also makes community participation visible beyond a service location. This is not a claim that everyone wants the same arrangement or that assistance removes every difficulty. Ask what control and connection mean to the person. Actual legal and program responsibilities remain distinct from the general principle introduced here.

slides.text:
Decision support preserves the person’s role
Chosen support can help people understand information, consider options, or communicate a position.

The support person’s preference is not automatically the individual’s decision.

Actual legal authority and information arrangements follow the relevant process.
slides.narration: A supporter may explain information or help compare possibilities while the person remains central. Ask what role is wanted rather than assuming that support means substitution. Someone may agree with a suggestion, disagree, or want time to think. Each response matters. This course does not determine legal capacity, guardianship, or the responsibilities of a specific service. In the learning, the question is how an arrangement preserves the person’s voice and avoids turning help into an automatic transfer of control.

slides.text:
A concern deserves detail, not a vague veto
A new activity may raise a specific practical or safety concern.

Name what is known, what support could be considered, and what requires qualified review.

Respecting choice does not mean dismissing responsibilities or treating every uncertainty as a reason to stop.
slides.narration: A general statement that something is unsafe can close the discussion without identifying the relevant issue. A specific concern about an unfamiliar travel route opens questions about information and support through the appropriate roles. Ignoring the concern would also fail to support an informed choice. Distinguish what is established from what needs examination. Repeated vague vetoes may keep familiar arrangements in place regardless of the person’s purpose. The learning cannot assess an actual risk or authorize an activity; it prepares clearer reasoning.

slides.text:
Compare the experience, not only the label
“Music activity” may mean watching, playing, choosing songs, or spending time with friends.

Explain relevant differences, support, availability, and unresolved questions.

A meaningful comparison can reveal that the familiar option meets only part of the goal.
slides.narration: A shared label can hide the features that matter most. The person may want to contribute to a group rather than simply hear music. An option might support that purpose while requiring more inquiry into access or timing. Another may be available but offer a different experience. Explain both honestly. This helps the person understand real choices without presenting uncertainty as approval or a familiar arrangement as the only conceivable path. The eventual preference and arrangement remain open until appropriately considered.

slides.text:
Development beyond the team’s usual course
An employee wants to deepen a relevant area of work. The discussion offers only the course the team has always used.

The default may overlook interests, prior knowledge, and a useful new direction.

Compare the desired capability, work needs, and realistic learning opportunities.
slides.narration: The workplace comparison is about development rather than a formal self-directed service. An employee can help define a learning direction while supervisors retain work responsibilities and actual resource decisions. A familiar course may still be suitable, but that should be examined rather than assumed. Repeating the default could narrow whose expertise develops in which areas. The next case asks how to make the employee’s purpose part of a realistic comparison. No approval, unlimited choice, or later development result is supplied.

slides.text:
Development directed toward a capability
An employee wants to deepen a relevant skill. Only the team’s familiar course is offered, without considering prior experience or other possibilities. Which response best supports development?
A. Require the usual course as proof of commitment.
B. Compare the desired capability, work needs, prior knowledge, and realistic options with the employee.
C. Let the employee choose anything and remove all work expectations.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The employee’s direction and organizational needs can be considered together. The usual course might be useful, but its familiarity does not establish that it fits the desired capability or prior experience. A development conversation can support meaningful influence without transferring every resource decision or removing work expectations. Consider which response opens an honest comparison. The fiction supplies no approved alternative or later performance result. It asks you to separate course activity from the purpose of learning and to retain what information is still needed to choose appropriately.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Require the usual course as proof of commitment.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Compare the desired capability, work needs, prior knowledge, and realistic options with the employee.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Let the employee choose anything and remove all work expectations.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A commitment test can replace inquiry about useful learning. Repetition may narrow development based on conformity to one path. Compare the actual capability and options; the course’s suitability is still unknown.

How would you distinguish finishing the course from developing the desired capability?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Requiring a familiar course as proof of commitment changes the question from what learning helps to whether the employee conforms. If repeated, that default may limit how varied experience develops into useful capability. Compare the course with the actual learning purpose and other realistic options. The case does not establish that the course is ineffective, that the employee lacks commitment, or that another option is approved.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This keeps the employee’s direction visible alongside relevant standards and resources. It may interrupt a habitual path that misses prior knowledge. Clarify the options; availability and later development effects remain unknown.

How would you distinguish finishing the course from developing the desired capability?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The comparison keeps personal direction and work responsibilities together. Prior knowledge and the desired capability can change what an option offers, while resources and standards remain relevant. This may interrupt a routine that treats one course as the only meaningful path. The response is an inquiry, not a guarantee. Suitability, approval, and what the employee eventually learns need information beyond the choice made here.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Removing expectations does not make the comparison useful for work. Repetition can create unclear commitments. Respect the goal while considering actual criteria and responsibilities; the preferred arrangement is not yet settled.

How would you distinguish finishing the course from developing the desired capability?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An employee’s interest matters, but removing all work expectations obscures the purpose of development and the actual decision responsibilities. An unlimited offer can create commitments that are unclear or unavailable. A supportive comparison names the capability, relevant options, and real constraints. The fiction does not settle what should be approved or whether any chosen activity will produce the desired learning result.

slides.text:
Choice can include a wish to retain the familiar
A person may prefer the current arrangement after considering alternatives.

Do not treat a new direction as automatically better or staying as lack of ambition.

Ask whether the preference is informed and whether useful options were genuinely available.
slides.narration: Respect for choice includes the possibility that someone values a familiar relationship or routine. Staff should not replace one default with pressure to choose novelty. At the same time, a stated preference may need to be understood in relation to what information and options were offered. If alternatives were never explained, the comparison is incomplete. Ask without leading toward your favored answer. The fiction does not establish why a person chooses to stay or whether the current arrangement meets every relevant need.

slides.text:
Life-course thinking can widen the conversation
Charting the LifeCourse resources can support exploration of a person’s vision, strengths, relationships, and supports.

Use the tool to open possibilities rather than prescribe a preferred life.

The person’s meaning remains central; completing a worksheet does not authorize services.
slides.narration: A visual tool can help someone explore connections that a service list misses. A relationship, community role, or interest may become visible alongside formal supports. The tool is useful when it serves the person’s thinking, not when staff use it to decide what a good life should look like. People may want different ways of exploring their goals. Appropriate responsibilities remain for actual planning and service decisions. The worksheet can support learning while leaving availability, agreement, and later experience uncertain.

slides.text:
Community knowledge reveals more than a service menu
Community engagement can reveal valued places, relationships, and participation beyond current service categories.

Briefs prepare questions about context; they do not determine an individual’s goals.

Seek varied voluntary perspectives without making one person a spokesperson.
slides.narration: A person’s desired life takes place among relationships and communities, not only within administrative categories. Engagement can help staff understand what opportunities mean and which conditions affect them. A brief may offer useful context about history or institutions while the individual explains their own interests. Avoid assuming that all members value the same activity or support. Repeated reliance on one familiar voice can narrow the picture. Community knowledge deepens inquiry without promising that every identified opportunity becomes an approved service.

slides.text:
Activity counts and personal outcomes differ
A service hour, visit, or written plan describes what was delivered.

A meaningful outcome concerns the person’s relationships, choices, participation, or desired experience.

Ask without leading; one result does not explain every cause or every person’s experience.
slides.narration: Activity information is useful for accountability, but it is not the same as knowing whether life moved in a direction the person wanted. A music session can occur without the person having a chance to contribute or connect. Ask about those features in terms the person understands. Their account may be mixed, and other influences may matter. Repeating activity counts as the only success measure can hide that difference. Preserve both the delivered support and what remains unresolved in the person’s experience.

slides.text:
A listening question already contains the answer
After a community activity, staff ask, “You enjoyed our wonderful session, didn’t you?”

The question may make disagreement harder and leave an unmet goal unheard.

Ask what fit, what differed, and what the person would want considered next.
slides.narration: A question can welcome an account or make one answer seem expected. Calling the session wonderful before asking may pressure the person to acknowledge staff effort instead of describing the experience. If repeated, reviews can report positive feedback while missing unresolved goals. A more open question makes room for both useful and difficult parts. The next choice asks how to hear that account without assuming every outcome is caused by the service or that an absence of criticism proves satisfaction.

slides.text:
Ask without directing the answer
After a community activity, staff ask, “You enjoyed our wonderful session, didn’t you?” The person had wanted more opportunity to contribute. Which question is more useful?
A. Ask them to confirm success because staff worked hard.
B. Count attendance as proof that the desired outcome occurred.
C. Ask what fit their purpose, what differed, and what they would want considered next.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The person can value part of an activity while still finding that another important part was absent. A leading question makes one answer easier to give and may hide that distinction. Consider whether the response seeks a meaningful account or reassurance about staff effort. Community perspectives can inform the review, but one account does not establish everyone’s outcome or a complete causal explanation. No revised activity or agreement is supplied. The strongest question leaves room for what fit, what did not, and what the person wants considered through the appropriate process.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Ask them to confirm success because staff worked hard.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Count attendance as proof that the desired outcome occurred.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Ask what fit their purpose, what differed, and what they would want considered next.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The request can make gratitude a condition of feedback. Repetition may hide unmet goals behind agreeable replies. Ask openly about the experience; appreciation and goal achievement are not the same evidence.

What wording would let a useful part and an unmet part both be heard?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Staff effort deserves respect, but it does not require the person to describe the outcome positively. Asking for confirmation can turn feedback into reassurance and leave an unmet purpose invisible. If repeated, reviews may preserve the same arrangement while reporting satisfaction. An open question can hear appreciation and difficulty together. The case does not establish what the person felt about every part or what change would be suitable.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Attendance describes an activity, not the person’s meaningful experience. Repetition may preserve a schedule that misses contribution. Ask about the desired outcome; attendance alone does not establish it.

What wording would let a useful part and an unmet part both be heard?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Attendance is evidence that an activity occurred, not that the person could contribute in the way they wanted. Treating it as the whole outcome can leave the service’s count more visible than the person’s life. Ask about relevant experience without leading or assigning a cause in advance. The case supplies participation and an unmet wish, but no complete evaluation or proof that the entire activity lacked value.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This makes mixed experience and changed preferences possible to hear. It may interrupt a review habit that favors reassurance. Keep the account’s scope and actual decision process clear; a later change is not yet established.

What wording would let a useful part and an unmet part both be heard?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The question allows the person to describe the relationship between the activity and their purpose. Mixed feedback can clarify a useful part and a remaining gap without denying staff effort. If maintained, this review approach may reduce reliance on activity counts alone. It still does not authorize a new arrangement or establish wider effects. The person’s later preference and the appropriate decision remain open.

slides.text:
Do not make gratitude a condition of being heard
A person can appreciate support and still want part of an arrangement changed.

Mixed feedback can clarify what matters rather than prove the effort failed.

Retain the person’s account without requiring reassurance or public appreciation.
slides.narration: Staff may have invested considerable effort in arranging an activity. That effort can be recognized without making the person responsible for reporting a positive outcome. Someone may enjoy the music and still miss the opportunity to play with others. Hear both parts. If feedback is repeatedly filtered through gratitude, the review may preserve the familiar arrangement even when a meaningful feature is absent. The account should inform appropriate next questions, not become proof that everything succeeded or that nothing had value.

slides.text:
Change may concern control as well as access
A usable activity can still leave a person without influence over timing, participation, or chosen support.

Ask which decision the person wants to help direct.

An access improvement and greater influence may support different parts of the goal.
slides.narration: Access and control can reinforce one another without being the same thing. A person may be able to attend yet have no say in the role they take or how support is involved. Describe the relevant choice and real constraints rather than announcing complete self-direction because the venue became usable. Repeating an arrangement with no meaningful influence may preserve the original problem in another form. The appropriate review can ask what the person wants to direct and which options are actually available.

slides.text:
Write a comparison that preserves the purpose
Choose the music, development, or feedback example.

Describe the person’s purpose, differences between real options, useful support, and one unresolved question.

What would be lost if the account contained only an activity label?
slides.narration: Use the practice situations so no personal record is needed. In the music example, distinguish attending from contributing and being with others. In the development example, distinguish course completion from the capability the employee wants to deepen. Add the information and relevant support needed to compare options. Keep real constraints and unknowns clear. Your reflection can remain private. The comparison helps you reason about meaningful choice without pretending to approve an arrangement or demonstrate a later outcome.

slides.text:
Review with room for a different direction
People may revise a goal after experience or changing circumstances.

Ask what the change means before calling it inconsistency or refusal.

Use the appropriate process for actual decisions and retain unanswered questions.
slides.narration: An experience may help someone understand what they value or discover that an activity differs from what they expected. Revising the goal can be meaningful information. Treating every change as noncompliance may keep people in arrangements that no longer fit. Ask what they want considered and explain actual limits accurately. The responsible process still governs service or work decisions. A revised preference does not automatically authorize a change, but neither should it disappear because staff already completed the earlier plan.

slides.text:
Keep life larger than the service list
Meaningful choice connects purpose, useful information, chosen support, and appropriate influence.

Recognize activity delivered while listening for the experience that matters to the person.

Continue with person-centered thinking, Charting the LifeCourse, and community resources when useful.
slides.narration: The central question is whether support serves the person’s life rather than becoming its only description. The cases connect that question with informed options, a development direction, and an honest account of experience. Keep the person’s influence visible alongside actual responsibilities and constraints. An unfamiliar possibility deserves inquiry without a guarantee, and a familiar preference deserves respect without assumption. Continued learning can help staff notice when a routine narrows choices and ask what would make the next conversation more meaningful.

outcomes: Explain self-direction and supported decision-making without equating support with taking control.
Distinguish a service delivered from an outcome that matters in the person’s life.
Explore strengths, relationships, and desired experiences beyond a service list.
Recognize when a routine limits choice because it treats one familiar arrangement as the safe or normal option.
